filaments.name: ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene)
filaments.summary: The classic engineering thermoplastic: tough, impact-resistant, usable near 95-100 °C and uniquely acetone-smoothable. In exchange it is the hardest of the commodity three to print — high shrinkage, real warping and delamination without a heated enclosure, poor UV life, and styrene fumes that demand ventilation.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $20-24, premium $28-35 per kg. ABS no longer undercuts PETG — budget PETG now often matches or beats it.

filaments.name: ABS-FR (Flame-Retardant ABS)

filaments.name: ABS-GF (Glass-Fiber-Filled ABS)
filaments.summary: ABS with its worst habit partly cured. filaments.name: LW-PLA (Lightweight Foaming PLA)
filaments.summary: Base PLA with a thermally activated foaming agent — the only PLA variant whose density is set by the operator rather than the spool. The cost is steep and non-linear: bending stiffness drops 3200 → 900 MPa and Z layer adhesion 33 → 4.3 MPa, so strength falls faster than weight. It also needs per-model temperature/flow calibration, prints hotter than any other PLA grade, and must not be annealed.

filaments.name: PEEK (Polyetheretherketone)
filaments.summary: The ceiling of FDM materials and the hardest thing in this catalog to print. Continuous-use temperature of 240-260 °C, Tg 143 °C and Tm 343 °C put it above every other entry here, and its chemical resistance is near-total. The cost is total hardware gating: a 375-410 °C industrial hotend that no Bambu machine (not even the X1E high-temp hotend at ~350 °C) can reach, an actively heated 70-140 °C chamber that is genuinely mandatory rather than merely helpful, non-standard build surfaces, and ~$400-900/kg. Deltas vs siblings: it beats pekk on peak temperature but loses to it on printability, layer adhesion and warp; it beats pei-ultem and ppsu on service temperature but loses to both on dimensional stability because it is semi-crystalline; and it loses to pps on raw chemical/solvent resistance while beating it comprehensively on Tg.

price.notes: 3DXTech ThermaX PEEK is the reference listing: $385/500 g (~$770/kg), $588/1 kg, $1,175/2 kg (~$588/kg). Broader market spans roughly $400-900/kg depending on brand and base resin grade (Victrex/Solvay-class resin at the top). Comparable to ppsu, roughly on par with or slightly above pekk, and 3-5x pei-ultem 1010 or pps.

filaments.name: PEI / ULTEM (Polyetherimide)
filaments.summary: The dimensionally sane member of the high-performance cluster. Being amorphous rather than semi-crystalline, it has no crystallisation shrinkage to fight, so it holds tolerances and welds layers better than peek or pekk — dimensional stability 8 and layer adhesion 8, the joint best here. Deltas vs peek: cheaper by 3-4x (ULTEM 1010 ~$195/kg against $400-900/kg), prints 20-40 °C cooler, warps far less, but tops out around 170-200 °C continuous instead of 240-260 °C. Deltas vs ppsu: essentially the same printing story and the same amorphous stability, but PEI is stiffer and stronger while PPSU is far tougher and better in steam and water. Its own weakness is moisture: it is the most hygroscopic material in this cluster, needing 110-150 °C drying and a dry box during the print, not just before it.

price.notes: ULTEM 1010 from 3DXTech: $98/500 g, $195/1 kg, $390/2 kg — comfortably the cheapest of the very-high-temperature group and roughly a third to a fifth of peek or ppsu. ULTEM 9085 is dearer at ~€256/kg (~$270-290/kg, Formfutura), and was listed as not available for sale at the time of checking, so that end of the band is soft.

recommended: aerospace interior and FST-rated parts (ULTEM 9085, UL94 V-0/5VA with low smoke and toxicity)
electrical and ESD-sensitive housings (ESD-safe 1010 variants exist)
dimensionally critical high-temperature parts where peek would warp
not_recommended: printers without a 400 °C-class hotend and heated chamber — Bambu machines included
the highest continuous-service-temperature applications, where peek, pekk and annealed pps-cf all lead
large square flat plates, which warp even with chamber heating
any workflow without drybox discipline through the whole print
outdoor and UV-exposed parts (weathering behaviour poorly documented)
food-contact items

filaments.name: PEKK (Polyetherketoneketone)
filaments.summary: PEEK's more printable cousin. The two-ketone structure crystallises far more slowly — roughly a 3.5-minute half-time at 250 °C against 1-2 minutes for PEEK — which is the whole story: lower internal stress, better layer welding, a genuinely wider processing window. Deltas vs peek: nozzle drops to 345-375 °C from 375-410 °C, Tg rises to 162 °C from 143 °C, warp and layer adhesion both improve markedly, and ease of print doubles from the catalog floor. It gives up a little peak stiffness and a little service temperature. Deltas vs the amorphous siblings: still warps more than pei-ultem and ppsu and still needs a chamber, but runs hotter in service than either. Like peek it is outside every consumer printer's hotend range, including Bambu's.

price.notes: 3DXTech ThermaX PEKK-A: $295/500 g (~$590/kg), $550/1 kg, $995/2 kg (~$497/kg). Comparative sources describe PEKK as 'inherently more expensive' than PEEK, but 3DXTech's own 1 kg PEKK price ($550) sits slightly BELOW their 1 kg PEEK price ($588) — so the premium claim is a generalised industry statement that does not hold for every brand. Recorded band covers the verified 3DXTech listings plus headroom for brands where the premium does apply.

recommended: defence parts requiring high-temperature performance with dimensional accuracy
high-temperature parts where print quality matters more than the last 20 °C of service temperature
large or geometrically awkward high-performance parts that peek would warp
inherently flame-retardant parts (UL94 V-0 without additives)
not_recommended: consumer and prosumer printers — the hotend range is out of reach, Bambu included
unheated-chamber setups
budget projects (~$500-700/kg)
absolute peak stiffness or service temperature, where peek still leads
food-contact items (no verification for printed parts)

filaments.name: PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate)
filaments.summary: The unmodified parent of PETG: stiffer, more heat-tolerant and more chemically resistant, but semi-crystalline, so it shrinks and warps as it crystallises rather than simply cooling. That single difference makes it markedly harder to print than PETG and explains why it stayed a niche material even though it is the world's most common polyester.

price.notes: Standard PET runs roughly $20-35/kg. Recycled grades are similar or slightly cheaper — FormFutura ReForm rPET is around EUR 16.50/kg (~$18/kg), while branded rPET spools commonly sit at $25-35/kg.

recommended: parts needing more stiffness and thermal headroom than PETG
general-purpose functional parts where stiffness outranks ease of printing
not_recommended: first prints or beginner projects (warp-prone and needs tuning)
large flat parts without an enclosure (severe corner lift from crystallisation shrinkage)
tight-tolerance parts on open-frame printers in uncontrolled ambient conditions
long unattended prints (needs closer monitoring than PETG)
printers without a bed that reaches 70-90 °C or without an all-metal hotend

filaments.name: PET-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled PET)
filaments.summary: The heat-resistant member of the filled-copolyester set. Deltas vs base pet: warp largely tamed by the fiber, tensile up to 74 MPa XY, and HDT 205 °C at 0.45 MPa against base PET's ~70 °C — but a hardened nozzle, a 260-290 °C nozzle, a 45-60 °C chamber, a sub-100 mm/s speed cap and no AMS. Against petg-cf it is the harder print by a wide margin and roughly 20-30 % dearer, bought for a heat ceiling petg-cf simply does not have.

price.notes: Bambu $35.99/kg (from $44.99). Roughly on par with or slightly above petg-cf, and Siraya Tech puts the category at 20-30 % above PETG-CF generally — around double base PET's $18-35/kg.

recommended: under-hood and other sustained-heat automotive parts
functional prototypes loaded at elevated temperature
parts that would creep or soften in petg-cf above ~70 °C
stiff structural brackets where Z loading can be designed out
not_recommended: beginner projects or first prints on an open-frame machine
AMS or multi-material slots (vendor-listed incompatible)
parts loaded in Z (Z tensile is under half of XY)
impact-prone or flexible parts
food-contact items
cosmetic parts (opaque matte black, fiber-flecked)

filaments.name: PETG (Glycol-Modified PET)
filaments.summary: The workhorse step up from PLA: tougher, far better layer adhesion, genuinely water-resistant and usable to ~70 °C, with only mild warp and no enclosure requirement. Pays for it with stringing, oozing, softer detail and supports that fuse hard to the part.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $22-26, premium $30-42 per kg. The historical price gap with ABS has closed — budget PETG now often matches or undercuts ABS.

recommended: outdoor brackets and enclosures (moderate UV exposure)
water bottles and non-potable liquid containment
parts where layer adhesion / Z-strength is critical
not_recommended: high-precision dimensional parts (more ooze and stringing than PLA)
parts with crisp overhangs or long bridges (sags and droops)
geometry needing easy support removal (supports fuse strongly)
under-hood or high-temperature applications (HDT ~68-80 °C)
fine-detail miniatures (glossy, stringy finish blurs detail)

filaments.name: PETG-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled PETG)
filaments.summary: Base PETG made stiff and dimensionally quiet by chopped carbon fiber. Deltas vs petg: tensile modulus roughly 5100 MPa against ~2000 MPa, warp and stringing both drop, and the surface goes matte black — paid for with a mandatory hardened nozzle, a lower speed ceiling (<150-200 mm/s vs PETG's 200+), sharply reduced elongation (~2 % vs 20 %+) and much weaker layer bonding. Unlike pet-cf it gains almost no heat resistance: HDT stays around 70 °C, the same as base PETG.

price.notes: Roughly 1.3-2x base PETG's $18-42/kg. Bambu $34.99/kg (discounted); eSUN, TINMORRY and generic brands $25-35/kg; premium US-made 3DXTech CarbonX runs $50/750 g (~$67/kg) or $120/2 kg (~$60/kg).

recommended: jigs, fixtures and tooling needing stiffness rather than heat resistance
flat, large-footprint parts where base PETG would bow
matte cosmetic-functional parts where PETG's gloss and stringing are unwanted
not_recommended: parts needing flexibility, impact toughness or snap-fit elasticity (elongation ~2 %)
clear or translucent parts (the fiber makes it opaque matte black)
food-contact items
sustained load above ~70 °C — the CF does not raise PETG's HDT (use pet-cf instead)
parts loaded in Z (Z tensile is roughly 65 % of XY)
0.2 mm nozzle detail work

filaments.name: PETG-ESD (Static-Dissipative PETG)
filaments.summary: Base PETG made static-dissipative for electronics work. Deltas vs petg: surface resistivity controlled to roughly 10⁴-10⁹ Ω, a hardened nozzle recommended because the conductive filler is mildly abrasive, a wider and hotter nozzle window (230-290 °C across brands against 220-250 °C), a pronounced Z-strength penalty (eSUN 48.1 MPa XY against 19.3 MPa Z), black only, and worse UV/ageing behaviour than base PETG's already-moderate rating. Price is the biggest delta of all: roughly $105-140/kg against base PETG's $18-42. Heat resistance is unchanged — HDT 76 °C.

price.notes: 3DXTech 3DXSTAT ESD-PETG at $105/750 g (~$140/kg) and $250/2 kg (~$125/kg); the 2 kg spool sets the low end near $105-125/kg. Roughly 4-6x base PETG's $18-42/kg — the premium is the conductive additive, not the copolyester. eSUN and Fiberon pricing was not captured (unverified), and cheaper grades likely exist.

recommended: ESD-safe jigs, fixtures and workbench tooling for electronics assembly
IC and PCB handling trays and carriers
static-dissipative guards and covers on production lines
replacing machined ESD plastics for low-volume fixtures
not_recommended: any part needing a colour other than black
outdoor or UV-exposed service (explicitly poor light and ageing resistance)
food-contact items
parts loaded in Z (Z tensile is roughly 40 % of XY)
high-temperature service (HDT 76 °C, no gain over base PETG)
cost-sensitive work where plain PETG would do

filaments.name: PETG-GF (Glass-Fiber-Filled PETG)
filaments.summary: The tougher, non-conductive counterpart to petg-cf. Deltas vs base petg: much higher stiffness and dimensional stability (<0.5 % change after annealing), a mandatory hardened nozzle, and — in the PET-based grades that dominate this category — a dramatically higher HDT of up to 133 °C annealed against base PETG's ~72 °C. Versus petg-cf it trades some stiffness for better layer bonding and impact toughness, keeps the surface electrically insulating, and is fussier about moisture.

price.notes: Comparable to or slightly cheaper than petg-cf: Polymaker Fiberon PET-GF15 $29.99/1 kg or $74.99/3 kg (~$25/kg); TINMORRY-branded PETG-GF in the same band. Glass fiber is cheaper to compound than carbon fiber, which is why the premium over base PETG is smaller than petg-cf's.

recommended: brackets and housings near electronics, where a non-conductive filler matters
parts needing stiffness with more impact tolerance than petg-cf offers
annealed parts serving above base PETG's ~70 °C ceiling
large flat functional prints where base PETG bows
not_recommended: cosmetic or aesthetic parts (matte, fiber-flecked surface)
flexible or energy-absorbing applications
food-contact items
parts printed on a PTFE-lined hotend if the grade runs near 300 °C
printers without a hardened nozzle
workflows without reliable dry storage

filaments.name: PLA (Polylactic Acid)
filaments.summary: The default FDM material and the easiest polymer to print: no enclosure, almost no warp, excellent dimensional accuracy and the lowest emissions of the common filaments. The trade-off is heat and weather: parts soften near 55-60 °C, creep under sustained load, and embrittle in sunlight.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $14-18, mid $18-22, premium/specialty $25-35 per kg

not_recommended: outdoor parts (UV embrittlement and discolouration)
sustained-load mechanical parts (creep)
anything in a hot car or near heat (softens above ~60 °C)
automotive/engine-bay parts
direct hot-liquid food contact
high-impact or drop-prone parts (brittle fracture)

filaments.name: PLA-CF (Carbon-Fibre Reinforced PLA)
filaments.summary: Base PLA filled with chopped carbon fibre — the stiffness-and-stability variant, and the only entry in this PLA set that is not a polylactide-class material. Versus base PLA it is denser (1.29 vs 1.24 g/cm³), stiffer (Young's modulus ~3280 MPa), warps less and holds dimensions better, and prints with a matte fibre texture that hides layer lines. The costs are a mandatory hardened nozzle, strongly reduced toughness, and the sharpest anisotropy in the PLA family (Bambu 38 MPa X-Y vs 26 MPa Z). Critically, it does NOT raise heat resistance: HDT is still ~54 °C.

price.notes: Bambu PLA-CF about $34.99/kg (US store listing, 1 kg spool assumed); Polymaker PolyLite PLA-CF about $29.99/kg (1 kg spool); eSUN PLA-CF in the same band (unverified). Roughly a $10-20/kg premium over base PLA, at or slightly above the pla-plus/lw-pla tier — and the hardened nozzle is an additional one-off cost.

recommended: parts needing high stiffness-to-weight and dimensional accuracy
parts with heavy support usage (supports release easily)
not_recommended: impact- or snap-loaded parts (worse than base PLA and much worse than pla-plus)
parts loaded in Z (26 MPa Z vs 38 MPa X-Y)
high-temperature parts — CF does NOT raise HDT here, still ~54 °C
exposure to strong acids or alkalis
smooth, injection-moulded-look surfaces (visible fibre texture)
printers without a hardened nozzle
food-contact items
outdoor parts

filaments.name: Glow-in-the-Dark PLA
filaments.summary: PLA carrying a strontium-aluminate phosphor that charges under light and glows in the dark. Printing temperatures are base-PLA-like (190-230 °C) and it has the best layer bonding of any filled variant in this cluster (Z 26 vs XY 32 MPa), but the phosphor is aggressively abrasive: a hardened nozzle is required, 0.2 mm nozzles are out, and it chews plastic AMS feeder components in a way base PLA never does.

price.notes: Bambu PLA Glow around $24.99/kg, matching pla-gradient and pla-wood and above base PLA at $18-20/kg. Budget for nozzle wear on top of filament cost

recommended: thick-walled parts where glow duration matters (target 2 mm or more)
not_recommended: fine-detail prints needing a 0.2 mm nozzle
printing on a shared or expensive hotend without a hardened nozzle fitted
high-volume AMS-fed jobs without feeder protection
load-bearing or structural parts
food-contact items
outdoor or hot-environment parts (base-PLA limits apply)

filaments.name: Gradient PLA
filaments.summary: Base PLA with a colour-blending manufacturing process and no chemistry change: pigment is graded along the strand so a tall print shifts colour with height. Printing, drying, feeding, mechanical and thermal behaviour are all base-PLA-equivalent; the only real deltas are price (~$25/kg vs ~$18-20/kg) and the design constraint that the part must be tall or long enough for the transition to develop.

price.notes: Bambu PLA Basic Gradient around $24.99/kg — roughly a 25-40 % premium over base PLA Basic ($18-20/kg) that buys the colour-blending process, not any material improvement

recommended: showpieces where colour transition across height is the design
single-material prints that need to look multi-colour without an AMS
not_recommended: small prints where the transition has no room to develop
batch prints needing consistent colour part-to-part
colour-critical engineering or coded parts
sustained-load, hot-environment or outdoor parts (same limits as base PLA)

filaments.name: High-Flow PLA (High-Speed PLA)
filaments.summary: Base PLA rheology-tuned for speed — same lactide chemistry, process delta only. Versus base PLA the melt is thinner and re-solidifies faster, lifting the usable speed band from roughly 40-100 mm/s to 100-300 mm/s (600+ mm/s on capable hardware) and volumetric flow from ~24 to ~28 mm³/s on Prusa's own comparison. Nozzle and bed temperatures are near-identical to base PLA and near-100 % part cooling becomes mandatory rather than merely advisable. Strength, heat resistance and weather behaviour are unchanged; the finish is glossier and less forgiving of defects than matte PLA.

price.notes: Prusament PLA High Speed about $29.90/kg (1 kg spool, Prusa store, confirmed); eSUN ePLA-HS sits in the eSUN PLA+/Basic band at roughly $18-23/kg (unverified). A modest $5-10/kg premium over base PLA, the same tier as pla-plus and below pla-cf/lw-pla.

recommended: large draft models where print time dominates
not_recommended: parts where a matte, defect-hiding finish matters (glossier and less forgiving than matte PLA)
high-temperature parts (no thermal improvement over base PLA)
sustained-load structural parts (creep, as with base PLA)
maximum-toughness parts (see pla-plus)
outdoor parts
food-contact items

filaments.name: Matte PLA
filaments.summary: Base PLA plus a light matting filler that kills gloss and visually hides layer lines and fingerprints. Versus base PLA it is denser (1.31 vs 1.24 g/cm³), runs 5-10 °C hotter and 10-20 % slower because the filler raises melt viscosity, and is somewhat weaker and more brittle (tensile XY 30 MPa vs 45-65 MPa) — everything else, including drying and warp behaviour, is base-PLA-equivalent.

price.notes: Bambu PLA Matte around $19.99-22.99/kg. The premium over base PLA has narrowed to marginal in recent years — cheaper than pla-gradient, pla-wood, pla-glow and pla-metal, which sit near $25/kg

recommended: parts where layer lines and fingerprints must not read
not_recommended: high-impact parts
snap-fit and clip geometry (more brittle than base PLA)
food-contact items (filler package uncertified)
sustained-load or outdoor parts, same as base PLA

filaments.name: Metal-Filled PLA
filaments.summary: PLA carrying metal powder so parts can be sanded and polished to a real metallic shine, and in the case of steel-filled grades are faintly magnetic and can be patinated. Versus base PLA it needs a hardened nozzle, is markedly more brittle, and the category splits sharply: light metallic-effect products (density ~1.25 g/cm³) print almost like base PLA, while true heavy-fill grades (bronzeFill 3.9, steelFill 3.13 g/cm³) demand 20-80 mm/s, wear brass nozzles out in ~1.5 kg, and drop elongation to 1-3 %.

price.notes: Two price tiers: Bambu PLA Metal around $24.99/kg (in line with pla-gradient, pla-wood and pla-glow), versus colorFabb bronzeFill/steelFill around $60-65/kg for genuine heavy metal-powder loading — 2-3x more. General metal-filled market pricing is quoted at $30-80/kg. Note that heavy-fill spools also yield far less volume per kilogram: 100 g of bronzeFill is only ~26 cm³ against ~80 cm³ for base PLA

recommended: visualisation prototypes with a metal look and heft
parts intended for sanding and polishing to a metallic shine
patinated finishes (liver of sulfur on copper/bronze, peroxide 'rusting' on steel)
not_recommended: load-bearing, snap-fit or impact-loaded parts (1-3 % elongation in heavy-fill grades)
fine thin walls or nozzles below 0.4 mm
long-Bowden or AMS-routed printing of heavy-fill grades
food-contact items
outdoor parts (exposed surface metal oxidises and streaks)

filaments.name: PLA+ (Toughened PLA)
filaments.summary: Base PLA plus a proprietary impact modifier — same lactide chemistry, mechanical delta only. Versus base PLA it trades some stiffness and tensile strength for markedly better impact toughness and layer adhesion (Bambu measures higher elongation in Z than in XY, the toughening signature), runs hotter at the top of the range (210-250 °C vs 190-230 °C), wants a hotter/longer dry (55 °C/8 h vs 45-55 °C/6 h) and prints slower than base PLA (eSUN and colorFabb recommend 40-50 mm/s). Heat resistance is unchanged: HDT still ~53-58 °C.

price.notes: eSUN PLA+ about $22.99/kg (1 kg spool, eSUN store, confirmed); Bambu PLA Tough+ about $29.99/kg and colorFabb Tough PLA about $40-45/kg (both unverified — store figures not confirmed by fetch). Roughly a $5-15/kg premium over base PLA's $14-35/kg band.

recommended: cosplay props needing more durability than base PLA
not_recommended: high-temperature parts (HDT still ~53-58 °C)
continuously loaded structural parts (creep, as with base PLA)
maximum-stiffness parts (see pla-cf)
high-throughput printing (see pla-hf)
outdoor parts
food-contact items

filaments.name: Silk PLA
filaments.summary: Base PLA with a gloss additive package — same lactide chemistry, aesthetic delta only. Versus base PLA it runs 10-20 °C hotter and slower for maximum sheen (210-240 °C vs 190-230 °C), is denser (1.27 vs 1.24 g/cm³), noticeably more moisture-sensitive, and has markedly worse layer adhesion (Z tensile 25 MPa vs XY 33 MPa) and low elongation (2.8 % XY), so it is a display material, not a structural one.

price.notes: Bambu PLA Silk+ around $22.99/kg; comparable to or slightly above base PLA Basic at roughly $18-20/kg

recommended: gifts and giveaway prints where finish sells the part
not_recommended: load-bearing or structural parts
snap-fit and clip geometry (low elongation, brittle)
parts loaded in Z (weak layer bonding)
food-contact items (additive/colourant package uncertified)
outdoor parts

filaments.name: Wood-Filled PLA
filaments.summary: PLA compounded with real wood fibre for a sandable, wood-look, wood-smelling part. Versus base PLA it needs a hardened nozzle, slower speeds (40-60 mm/s) and more retraction, is lighter (1.21 vs 1.24 g/cm³), and is much weaker and more anisotropic (tensile XY 26 MPa, Z 15 MPa vs 45-65 MPa base). It is also the worst of the six aesthetic variants outdoors, because the fibre absorbs water independently of the PLA.

price.notes: Bambu PLA Wood around $24.99/kg — a moderate premium over base PLA at $18-20/kg, in line with pla-gradient and pla-glow

recommended: parts intended to be sanded, stained or finished like wood
props where a wood grain look and smell sells the piece
not_recommended: load-bearing or structural parts
impact-prone or drop-prone parts
snap-fit and clip geometry
parts loaded in Z (Z tensile is roughly half XY)
fine thin walls or 0.2 mm nozzle detail work (fibre clogs)
food-contact items
unsealed outdoor use (fibre swells and degrades)

filaments.name: PP (Polypropylene)
filaments.summary: The living-hinge and chemical-resistance specialist: light, flexible, fatigue-resistant and essentially waterproof, with the lowest density of the common filaments so a spool yields the most part volume. It is also one of the hardest materials to print — extreme warping and near-universal non-adhesion mean it needs its own build surface, since the same non-stick behaviour that makes PP tape a great release layer for other materials makes PP itself refuse to stick to anything.

price.notes: 2025-2026 standard PP filament: Fiberlogy PP around €51/kg (~$55/kg); 0.75-1 kg spools commonly $30-55 each on the wider market. Precise current USD range unverified.

recommended: living hinges for snap-together boxes and lids
parts subject to repeated flexing and fatigue
not_recommended: high-precision dimensional parts (severe warping and shrinkage)
rigid structural load-bearing parts (low strength and stiffness)
parts relying on out-of-box bed or support adhesion
glued or solvent-welded assemblies (PP resists most adhesives and solvents)
fine-detail miniatures (poor first-layer control on most surfaces)
UV-exposed outdoor parts on non-stabilised grades

filaments.name: PP-GF (Glass-Fiber-Filled Polypropylene)
filaments.summary: Glass fiber is added to polypropylene less for stiffness than for restraint. Deltas vs the base pp entry: the fiber directly suppresses PP's defining crystallisation shrinkage, so warp_tendency drops from 10 — the catalog's worst — to 4, HDT@0.45 MPa rises from ~95 °C to 127 °C with service to 120 °C, and XY tensile roughly doubles to 41.7 MPa. What it does NOT fix is the other half of PP's difficulty: the material still refuses to stick to standard build surfaces and needs a PP-specific tape, sheet or primer, and the fiber adds a hardened-nozzle requirement base PP does not have. Vs the CF nylons in this cluster it is the coolest-running and lowest-temperature-ceiling option, but has the best water tolerance of the four by a wide margin.

price.notes: Wide and poorly documented in USD. Recreus PPGF at EUR 48.95/600 g works out to roughly $86/kg equivalent; BCN3D PP-GF30 at EUR 139.95/700 g is roughly $214/kg equivalent, a printer-specific certified product priced well above the general-purpose alternatives. Mid-tier industrial lines (BASF Ultrafuse, Fiberthree) are expected to land in an $80-150/kg band, but neither publishes pricing on the pages fetched, so that estimate is unverified. Against the base pp entry's $40-70/kg this is a 2-3x premium.

recommended: automotive and aerospace structural brackets, bars, shafts and frames
parts for harsh, humid or chemically aggressive environments
weather-exposed outdoor components (BCN3D cites UV and water resistance)
chemical-handling and fluid-adjacent hardware needing more stiffness than base PP
large flat PP parts that would be unprintable unfilled
housings and fixtures that must resist moisture indefinitely
not_recommended: high-precision small parts needing isotropic strength (ZX tensile is 38 % of XY)
living hinges and repeated-flex parts — the fiber destroys exactly the fatigue behaviour base pp is chosen for
food-contact vessels: no food-safe certification was found for any PP-GF filament
continuous service above ~120 °C — the lowest temperature ceiling in this cluster
printing on stock PEI, glass or standard build surfaces without a PP-specific tape, sheet or primer
brass-nozzle printers and 0.4 mm-only setups where BASF recommends 0.6 mm
glued or solvent-welded assemblies (inherited from base PP)

filaments.name: PPA (Polyphthalamide / High-Temp Nylon)
filaments.summary: The high-temperature tier of the polyamide family and the hardest material in this catalog outside the PEEK class. Deltas vs the base pa entry: melting point ~305 °C against PA6's ~220 °C, Tg 125 °C against ~50 °C, HDT from 196 °C @1.8 MPa (Bambu PPA-CF) to 260 °C (3DXTech PPA-GF15), tensile up to 168 MPa X-Y, and saturated water absorption of only ~1.3 %. It pays for all of it with the family's most extreme process window: 280-390 °C nozzle, 100-160 °C bed, a heated chamber, a hardened nozzle and 100-140 °C drying — plus roughly triple the price of pa6.

price.notes: The most expensive grade in the polyamide family by a wide margin — roughly 2-3x filled PA6 and 3-5x unfilled pa6. Bambu PPA-CF is $149.99/750 g (~$200/kg); 3DXTech FibreX PPA-GF15 is ~EUR 140/750 g (~$200/kg), falling to ~EUR 126-168/kg at 10+ units. Both figures are for fiber-filled grades because neat PPA filament is essentially not sold at retail.

recommended: jigs and fixtures for continuous high-temperature service
metal-replacement parts where pa66 lacks the heat capability
not_recommended: any printer without a heated chamber and a 300 °C+ all-metal hotend
consumer filament dryers that cannot reach 100 °C
budget or hobby projects — 3-5x the cost of pa6
parts needing high elongation or impact toughness (Z tensile is ~1/3 of X-Y)
large flat parts printed in a passive enclosure
food-contact items

filaments.name: PPA-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled Polyphthalamide)
filaments.summary: The high-temperature end of the CF-nylon family and the hardest print of the four composites in this cluster. Deltas vs the base pa entry: XY tensile 168±4 MPa against unfilled PA's ~52 MPa, HDT@0.45 MPa 227 °C against ~80 °C, and an explicit 50-80 °C chamber-temperature specification no other polyamide entry carries. Vs siblings: highest strength, stiffness and heat resistance of the trio, but the worst anisotropy (168 MPa XY against 57 MPa Z, a ~3:1 gap, so layer_adhesion falls to 3), the most aggressive drying schedule in the catalog (100-140 °C for 8-12 h), the hottest nozzle (280-315 °C) and the highest price (~$172-266/kg).

price.notes: The most expensive entry in this cluster and one of the most expensive filaments in the catalog. Bambu PPA-CF at $149.18/750 g (~$198.90/kg on 3DJake); P3D cites $129-150 per 0.75 kg spool (~$172-200/kg) and calls it 'one of the most expensive high-performance 3D printing filaments on the market'. 3DXTech CarbonX HTN+CF runs $200/750 g (~$266/kg) or $425/2 kg (~$212.50/kg). Roughly 2-3x pa6-cf.

recommended: under-hood automotive brackets under sustained high temperature
industrial tooling and jigs in hot or chemically aggressive environments
aerospace fixtures and high-load structural mounts
parts that must survive sustained exposure near 200 °C
high-load parts that can be oriented so the load runs in-plane
metal-replacement brackets where pa6-cf's heat ceiling is the limiting factor
not_recommended: anything printable adequately in pa6-cf or pa12-cf — the cost premium is 2-3x
beginners and non-enclosed printers: without chamber heat the layer bond is poor
parts loaded in Z without annealing (Z tensile is 34 % of XY, the worst gap in this cluster)
0.2 mm nozzle detail work — explicitly unsupported
printers whose hotend tops out below ~300 °C
workflows without a blast oven for the 100-140 °C drying schedule
food-contact items

filaments.name: PPS (Polyphenylene Sulfide)
filaments.summary: The chemical-resistance specialist of the high-performance cluster, and the cheapest entry in it at roughly $140-200/kg. Nothing else in this catalog matches its solvent and chemical resistance, and flame retardancy comes free with the chemistry rather than from additives. The catch is a Tg of just 85 °C — lower than pc's 145 °C and only marginally above pla's world — so although Tm is 285 °C, practical stiffness falls away far earlier than the peek/pekk/pei numbers suggest. Deltas vs siblings: best-in-class chemical, solvent and water tolerance (10/10), worst-in-class Tg, and semi-crystalline warp behaviour that puts it closer to peek than to the amorphous pair. Its own carbon-filled variant pps-cf fixes most of the warp and stiffness problems and is the grade most engineering users actually buy.

price.notes: 3DXTech ThermaX PPS 500 g spools: $70 at 2.85 mm (~$140/kg) and $100 at 1.75 mm (~$200/kg) — the diameter premium is the whole spread. This makes PPS the cheapest material in the high-performance cluster: below pei-ultem 1010 ($195/kg) at the 2.85 mm end, and a fraction of peek, pekk or ppsu at $400-900/kg.

recommended: chemical processing components exposed to aggressive solvents
electrical and electronics housings needing inherent flame retardance
parts that must survive immersion or sustained humidity
cost-sensitive high-performance work where peek is out of budget
not_recommended: structural parts operating above ~85 °C without reinforcement or annealing (Tg is the limiting factor, not Tm)
large flat geometry without careful bed and chamber control
printers below ~365 °C hotend capability — use the pps-cf variant at 310-350 °C instead
stiffness-critical parts, where pps-cf is the obvious upgrade
food-contact items (not verified for printed parts)

filaments.name: PPS-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled PPS)
filaments.summary: The grade of PPS that engineering users actually buy. Deltas vs the base pps entry: nozzle drops from 365-390 °C to 310-350 °C — low enough to land inside the X1E/H2D high-temp hotend's reach and make this the only member of the high-performance cluster with a real consumer-printer path — warp tendency falls from 9 to 3 with Fiberon stating no heated chamber or enclosure is needed at all, dimensional stability climbs from 5 to 8, and HDT reaches 252-264 °C after annealing where unfilled PPS has no published figure at all. It is paid for with a mandatory hardened nozzle, spool brittleness that rules out AMS use, and layer adhesion that drops BELOW the unfilled base (5 vs 6) — Z-axis tensile is 32 MPa against 87 MPa in XY, the most pronounced anisotropy in this cluster.

price.notes: Not confirmed from a primary listing in this research pass (unverified). The recorded band is the general market range for carbon-fiber-reinforced high-performance filament and is anchored by the observation that the PPS base resin is far cheaper than PEEK's, so PPS-CF should sit well below PEEK-CF pricing and roughly alongside the base pps entry's $140-200/kg. Treat both ends as estimates.

recommended: electronics assemblies needing flame retardance and chemical resistance
jigs, fixtures and shop tooling requiring metal-like stiffness
functional prototypes and end-use parts on machines without a heated chamber
chemically aggressive environments where stiffness also matters
high-HDT parts after annealing (252-264 °C at 0.45 MPa)
not_recommended: parts loaded in Z or needing isotropic strength (Z tensile 32 MPa vs 87 MPa XY)
impact-loaded or tough applications — the fiber trades toughness for stiffness
electrically insulating applications (carbon fiber is conductive — use a PPS-GF grade)
AMS or multi-material stations (brittle strand, tight bends snap it)
brass-nozzle printers
parts used at high temperature without the post-print annealing step that the HDT figures depend on

filaments.name: PPSU (Polyphenylsulfone)
filaments.summary: The tough, steam-proof member of the high-performance cluster. Tg 220 °C is the highest here — above both ULTEM grades — and it survives 1,000+ steam sterilisation cycles while meeting ISO 10993 biocompatibility, which nothing else in this cluster claims. Deltas vs pei-ultem: same amorphous low-warp behaviour and the same 8/8 stability-and-adhesion profile, a gentler 110 °C drying spec against 1010's 150 °C, far better impact toughness and water tolerance (10 vs 6), but lower stiffness and compressive strength (6 vs 7) and roughly double the price. Deltas vs peek: comparative sources put it behind on compressive strength, tensile strength and elasticity, and its 180 °C continuous rating is well short of PEEK's 240-260 °C — but it is easier to print, warps far less, and takes an impact that would crack a PEEK part.

price.notes: Estimated from Formfutura's ~€190/500 g listing, which works out above $400/kg. That puts PPSU among the most expensive materials in this cluster — broadly comparable to peek and above ULTEM 9085, and roughly 2-3x pei-ultem 1010 at $195/kg. The upper end is headroom for other brands rather than a verified listing.

recommended: sterilisable medical and surgical components (1,000+ steam cycles, ISO 10993)
plumbing and piping fittings, valves and connectors
aerospace parts needing impact resistance alongside chemical stability
parts exposed to hot water, steam or repeated autoclaving
high-temperature parts where toughness matters more than stiffness
not_recommended: printers without a 400 °C-class hotend and an actively heated 65 °C+ chamber — Bambu machines included
maximum stiffness or compressive strength at temperature, where peek and pekk lead
sustained service above ~180 °C
budget-sensitive work — pei-ultem 1010 delivers similar printing behaviour for a third of the price
parts with heavy support requirements (support removal is noted as difficult)
food-contact items without a certified line and post-print sealing

filaments.name: PVA (Polyvinyl Alcohol)
filaments.summary: The classic water-dissolvable support material, used almost exclusively as the second extruder in multi-material prints rather than as a build material. It pairs best with PLA at similar print temperatures, but it is extremely hygroscopic: unprotected filament can absorb enough moisture in a couple of hours to clog, string, or fail mid-print.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades. Budget brands (eSUN) sit at the low end, roughly $50-70/kg equivalent on 0.5 kg spools; premium brands (Prusament) reach or exceed the top of the range. Most PVA ships as 0.5 kg spools, so per-spool cost looks lower than per-kg.

recommended: dissolvable supports for complex overhangs and internal channels
supports for PLA prints (the best-established pairing)
hollow and nested geometries requiring full support dissolution
multi-material aesthetic PLA prints needing clean support interfaces
enclosed cavity supports that cannot be reached mechanically
not_recommended: standalone functional or load-bearing parts (weak and water-sensitive)
outdoor or humid-environment parts
long multi-day prints without a dry box or AMS (degrades mid-print)
supports for ABS/ASA/PC (poor adhesion and mismatched print temperatures)
food-contact parts

filaments.name: PVB (Polyvinyl Butyral)
filaments.summary: A PLA-easy filament whose whole reason for existing is post-processing: brief exposure to isopropyl alcohol melts the layer lines into a glossy, near-glass finish, and the same solvent welds parts together seamlessly. In exchange it is brittle in Z, hygroscopic, heat-limited, and dissolves on contact with alcohol or many household cleaners.

price.notes: Roughly double standard PLA. Prusament PVB is $24.99 per 500 g spool (~$50/kg); the wider market sits around $33-45/kg.

recommended: artistic pieces intended for IPA vapour smoothing to a glass-like finish
multi-part assemblies bonded seamlessly by alcohol welding
not_recommended: structural or load-bearing parts (weak layer adhesion, brittle fracture)
anything contacting alcohol, perfume or household cleaners (the material dissolves)
outdoor parts (no UV stabilisation, low heat resistance)
high-temperature applications (HDT ~60-68 °C)
parts that must hold tolerances after any solvent contact
food-contact items

filaments.name: TPE (Thermoplastic Elastomer)
filaments.summary: The softer, cheaper, more rubbery sibling of TPU: SEBS-based grades feel closer to real rubber, resist water and mild chemicals well, and several lines carry food and skin-contact certification. In exchange they are much weaker in tension than TPU, want very slow speeds with the fan off, and the 'TPE' label covers formulations different enough that datasheet numbers barely agree.

price.notes: Typically $25-45/kg (eSUN TPE-83A at $36.99/kg). Several sources note TPE runs slightly cheaper than equivalent TPU — 3D Insider describes eSUN Elastic TPE as a 'slightly less expensive alternative' to NinjaFlex TPU. Specialty and certified grades run higher; upper bound unverified.

recommended: phone and device cases and grips
wearable bands and straps with skin contact
not_recommended: structural or load-bearing parts
high-precision mechanical parts
applications above roughly 80 °C
parts needing high tensile strength (much weaker than TPU)
abrasion- or oil-exposed parts (SEBS is weaker here than polyester-based TPU)

filaments.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
filaments.summary: The default flexible filament: a rubbery block copolymer that prints on any direct-drive machine at room temperature with essentially no warp, and absorbs impact and vibration that rigid filaments transmit. The difficulties are all in feeding and tuning — it buckles in Bowden paths, needs slow speeds and retraction work, drinks moisture, and is markedly weaker in Z than XY.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard 85A-95A grades: budget generic ~$20-25, Bambu TPU ~$25-30, premium NinjaTek Cheetah and specialty soft grades $50-70+ per kg. Bounds unverified — flexible filament retail pricing is not consistently published per kilogram.

recommended: wearables such as watch bands and orthotic inserts
cable strain reliefs and protective sleeving
not_recommended: rigid structural or load-bearing parts
high-temperature applications
tight-tolerance mating parts (elastic recovery causes dimensional drift)
large flat parts (bed adhesion and removal are awkward)
food-contact use on uncertified grades

filaments.name: TPU 60A (ultra-soft flexible)
filaments.summary: The softest commonly sold FDM-printable TPU, and the hardest to print. Delta vs base TPU: hard-segment content drops to give a silicone-like 60A instead of the base entry's 85A-95A band, elongation at break roughly doubles to ~950%, print speed collapses to 10-20 mm/s, retraction must go to zero, and the nozzle runs hotter (~235 °C) than a typical 95A to keep the very-low-viscosity melt moving. Feeding is the whole problem: Bowden paths are ruled out entirely, a spool-side feeding assistant is close to mandatory, and Bambu's own guide puts 75A-and-below in the 'should not be printed' bucket, so this grade is off the table on those machines.

price.notes: The reference product, Recreus Filaflex 60A Pro, is a premium SKU at $57.90 per 500 g, i.e. roughly $116/kg. Generic 'TPU 60A' from budget suppliers is cited around $40-60/kg but exact figures for those brands are unverified. This is the most expensive grade in the family — the base entry's $20-70 band does not reach the top end here.

recommended: soft seals and gaskets needing high compression recovery
not_recommended: any load-bearing or structural part
dimensionally precise or tight-tolerance parts
Bambu printers and any material-station / AMS slot
Bowden-fed machines
all-metal hotends (per Recreus)
fast or unattended production runs

filaments.name: TPU 60D (semi-rigid)
filaments.summary: Semi-rigid TPU that behaves more like a tough engineering plastic than a flexible: hockey-puck stiffness with TPU's impact resistance and a little flex left over. Delta vs base TPU: this sits above the base entry's entire 85A-95A band on a different hardness scale, so the feeding problems largely disappear — Bowden becomes viable, no feeding assistant, near-PETG speeds — while the bed runs hotter at 50-60 °C and rubbery compression recovery is traded away. It is the stiffest, most dimensionally stable grade in the family apart from 68D, and the cheapest.

price.notes: Extrudr TPU hard runs about $44.62/kg ($33.46 per 750 g), while generic TPU-60D from Polar Filament is roughly $25-29/kg — a near-2x spread between name brand and generic at the same nominal durometer. This is the cheapest grade in the family and the only one whose floor reaches the base entry's $20-25 budget band.

recommended: tool and device cases needing shock absorption plus structure
gears and mechanical parts with impact tolerance
snap-fit and clip parts needing more rigidity than 95A
wear parts where TPU's abrasion resistance beats PETG
not_recommended: parts needing true rubber-like compression or squish (use 60A or 85A)
fully rigid structural parts (use a rigid engineering plastic)
applications where brand-to-brand durometer variance would matter
high-temperature service

filaments.name: TPU 68D (AMS-grade rigid flexible)
filaments.summary: TPU engineered backwards from a feeding problem: stiff enough to run through a material station without buckling, which makes it the only flexible-adjacent grade that can sit in an AMS slot alongside PLA and PETG. Delta vs base TPU: it inverts the base entry's defining constraints — AMS goes from a firm 'no' to 'yes', drive system from 'required' to 'any', the bed runs cooler at 30-35 °C rather than 45 °C, and density rises to a documented 1.26 g/cm³. What it gives up is rubberiness and, critically, Z-axis strength: 31% breaking elongation in Z against over 650% in XY, the most extreme anisotropy documented anywhere in the family.

price.notes: Bambu TPU for AMS is about $38.79/kg for a 1 kg spool at 3DJake — notably cheaper than Bambu's own TPU 85A/90A at roughly $60/kg, which likely reflects easier and faster manufacturing of the more rigid grade. Sits below the base entry's midpoint.

recommended: multi-colour and multi-material AMS prints needing a flexible accent
semi-rigid components printed alongside rigid filaments in one job
parts needing moderate flex with good in-plane strength
not_recommended: parts loaded in tensile across layers (31% Z elongation vs >650% XY)
applications needing rubbery compression or squish (use 60A or 85A)
high-temperature service (no HDT published)
food-contact use

filaments.name: TPU 85A (soft flexible)
filaments.summary: The soft end of the mainstream flexible range: gel-insole firmness, appreciably easier to feed than 60A but still the slowest and fussiest of the grades people actually buy in volume. Delta vs base TPU: this is the bottom of the base entry's 85A-95A band, so it prints slower (15-20 mm/s), wants retraction at or near zero, and adds a hardware gate the base entry does not record — Bambu's guide requires a 0.6 mm or 0.8 mm nozzle for TPU 85A and rules out 0.4 mm and 0.2 mm. Printable directly on Bambu machines unlike 60A, but still barred from the AMS.

price.notes: Bambu sells TPU 85A and 90A as one bundle line at roughly $54-60/kg (1 kg spool at about $59.99 direct; $53.99 CAD / €59.99 / £59.99 regionally). NinjaFlex 85A sits in a similar $50-70/kg band, exact per-kg figure unverified. Both are above the base entry's $20-70 midpoint — there is no true budget 85A in the way there is a budget 95A.

not_recommended: AMS or other material-station slots (bending/feeding failures)
0.4 mm or 0.2 mm nozzles (per Bambu's 85A guide)
fine-detail or dimensionally tight parts
high-speed or production-volume runs
structural or load-bearing parts

filaments.name: TPU 90A (medium-soft flexible)
filaments.summary: The middle of the mainstream flexible range — gummy-bear to soft-shoe-sole firmness, and the point where TPU stops fighting the printer. Delta vs base TPU: it sits inside the base entry's 85A-95A band, but prints faster than 85A (20-30 mm/s), tolerates a small 0-1 mm retraction instead of none, and drops 85A's nozzle-diameter gate entirely — Bambu lists 90A as compatible with 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm nozzles. Still barred from the AMS, and still direct-drive.

price.notes: Bambu bundles TPU 90A with TPU 85A at the same price — roughly $54-60/kg, 1 kg spool at about $59.99. Identical pricing to the 85A entry is not an error: the two are one product line. Generic 90A is less commonly stocked than generic 95A, which is why the low end does not reach the base entry's $20/kg floor.

recommended: protective housings needing more structure than 85A
not_recommended: AMS or other material-station slots
rigid or structural parts
tight-tolerance mating parts
applications wanting true rubbery squish (use 85A or 60A)

filaments.name: TPU 95A (standard flexible)
filaments.summary: The industry-standard flexible and the grade most people mean when they say 'TPU': firm shoe-sole feel, the best balance of flexibility against printability in the Shore A family. Delta vs base TPU: this is the firm end of the base entry's 85A-95A band and is where its caveats relax — speed climbs to 25-45 mm/s, limited retraction of 0.5-2 mm works, and a short well-constrained Bowden path is survivable, so drive_system is recorded as recommended rather than required. Still barred from the AMS, and still the best-documented grade for actual numbers.

price.notes: Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95 at $29.99 per 0.75 kg works out to about $40/kg. NinjaTek Cheetah 95A and the near-sibling Fillamentum Flexfill 92A sit in a $40-70/kg band across retailers, exact per-kg figures unverified. Cheaper than 85A/90A because 95A is the volume grade every brand stocks; the base entry's $20-25 budget-generic floor is plausible for no-name 95A but was not confirmed by these sources.

recommended: general-purpose flexible parts where no specific durometer is called for
not_recommended: AMS or other material-station slots
applications needing rubber-like softness (use 85A or 60A)
near-rigid or semi-structural parts (use 60D or 68D)
tight-tolerance press fits

manufacturers.name: 3DJake (niceshops GmbH)
manufacturers.summary: Austrian pan-European 3D printing retailer operated by niceshops GmbH that also sells a 3DJAKE house-brand filament range - ecoPLA, easyPETG, mattePLA, ABS, ASA, PCTG, TPU A95, niceBIO, magicPLA and mysteryPLA. The house line is marketed as 'Made in EU' with no disclosed contract manufacturer, making 3DJake a label rather than a verified extruder; the storefront simultaneously resells Devil Design, Spectrum, ROSA3D, Fiberlogy, FormFutura and Extrudr.

manufacturers.name: 3DXTECH
manufacturers.summary: US engineering-filament producer based in Grand Rapids, Michigan, running a 68,000 sq ft ISO 9001:2015-certified plant. Makes everything it sells in-house, from commodity PLA/PETG up to ultra-performance PEEK, PEKK and PEI, plus carbon- and glass-filled composites, ESD-safe grades and pellets. Sub-brands cover product families rather than separate companies: Triton3D (Stratasys-compatible spools), 3DXLabs, ThermaX, CarbonX, OBSIDIAN and 3DXSTAT.

manufacturers.name: add:north (Add North 3D AB)
manufacturers.summary: Swedish filament brand based in Olsremma, marketing its range as 'Made in Sweden' with heavy Nordic-origin and sustainability positioning. Catalogue centres on named PLA grades (X-PLA, E-PLA), PETG including an Economy line, the Rigid X engineering grade, TPU and the Addlantis nylon line. Reviewed as a top-tier premium brand.

manufacturers.name: Amolen
manufacturers.summary: Colour- and character-led consumer filament brand founded in 2017 and operating from Los Angeles, California. With roughly four employees it is a brand/import company rather than an extruder; manufacturing is outsourced and almost certainly Chinese, though no factory or OEM has been confirmed.

manufacturers.name: Shenzhen Anycubic Technology Co., Ltd.
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen printer maker founded 2015 by Lu Ouyang (CEO) and James Ouyang, operating in both FDM (Kobra series) and resin/SLA. Sells house-brand filament and resin alongside its hardware. Whether Anycubic extrudes filament itself or contracts it out is unresolved: a single low-confidence company-profile source names eSUN as a filament supplier, but this is uncorroborated and absent from the owner-verified ground-truth table, so no OEM relationship is encoded.

manufacturers.name: Atomic Filament
manufacturers.summary: Founder-operated US filament extruder in Kendallville, Indiana, started in 2014. Every spool is manufactured in-house and the brand positions on tight diameter control (claimed +/-0.02 mm) plus specialty UV-reactive and shade-shifting colors.

manufacturers.name: AzureFilm d.o.o.
manufacturers.summary: Slovenian filament manufacturer registered in Sezana with operations in Ljubljana, founded by the Derman family (brand launched 2014, family enterprise roots from 1968). Unusually, it builds its own extrusion lines and tooling in-house (mold making, injection molding, CNC milling), sells 3D printers alongside filament, and offers private-label/OEM production to third-party brands - making it a potential upstream OEM as well as a retail brand.

manufacturers.name: Bambu Lab (拓竹 Tuozhu)
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen-based consumer 3D printer company founded August 2020, best known for the X1/P1/A1 series and the AMS multi-material system. Bambu-branded filament is not produced in Bambu's own extrusion plants: per owner-verified records it is OEM-produced/resold via Sunlu and eSUN/Polymaker, all of whom manufacture in China. Catalog is broad (PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU, PA/PA-CF, PC, PVA and dedicated support materials) and tightly integrated with Bambu's RFID/AMS ecosystem.

manufacturers.name: COEX LLC (COEX 3D)
manufacturers.summary: Green Bay, Wisconsin manufacturer with an unusual origin: a plastic spiral book-binding producer operating since 1996 that pivoted its PVC monofilament extrusion expertise into FDM filament in 2016. Manufactures everything in-house on 100% virgin resins, with an engineering-leaning catalog including its own CoexFlex TPE and CoexNylex nylon lines.

manufacturers.name: colorFabb B.V.
manufacturers.summary: Dutch filament maker operating a dedicated 4,100 m2 factory in Belfeld, Netherlands (opened January 2017) that houses production, R&D and logistics. Known for specialty fill materials (woodFill, bronzeFill, copperFill, steelFill), the varioShore variable-density TPU, and recycled/biodegradable lines. Long associated with the Ultimaker ecosystem.

manufacturers.name: Comgrow (Shenzhen ZCSW Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Hong Kong-registered multi-brand 3D printing retailer founded in 2017, operating under the mainland entity Shenzhen ZCSW Technology Co., Ltd. Comgrow is an authorised Creality distributor that resells Creality filament (project-owner verified) and also sells own-brand COMGROW filament and accessories; it is a reseller/accessory brand rather than an independent extruder. A 2024 announcement indicates a merger with the related Sovol brand.

manufacturers.name: Shenzhen Creality 3D Technology Co., Ltd. (深圳市创想三维科技股份有限公司)
manufacturers.summary: Founded 2014 in Shenzhen and one of the largest consumer FDM hardware makers in the world (Ender, CR, K-series, Sermoon, HALOT resin). Unlike most printer brands, Creality extrudes its own filament in-house at scale and also acts as the OEM behind the Soleyin filament label. Catalog spans budget commodity PLA through Hyper high-speed lines and filled specialty variants.

manufacturers.name: DAS FILAMENT
manufacturers.summary: Small German filament manufacturer in Emskirchen, Bavaria, registered as a sole proprietorship (Roman Stieben, DAS FILAMENT). States that all its filaments are developed and produced in Germany. Notable for offering both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm diameters, uncommon among current European premium brands, and for targeting the German-language maker market rather than global distribution.

manufacturers.name: Devil Design (Devil Design Sp. J.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament producer based in Mikolow, Silesia, marketed in Polish retail as a 'Polski producent filamentu' (Polish filament manufacturer). Filament-only catalogue covering PLA, PET-G, ABS+, ASA, PA12, HIPS and TPU in 1 kg, 2 kg and bulk 5 kg formats, sold direct and through an unusually broad electronics-distribution channel (TME).

manufacturers.name: Duramic 3D
manufacturers.summary: Small Amazon-centric consumer filament label selling a PLA-heavy range plus PETG and TPU. Corporate ownership, headquarters and factory are not disclosed anywhere public; Duramic 3D appears to be a reseller of contract-manufactured filament rather than a producer, but no sourcing statement of any kind was found.

manufacturers.name: ELEGOO
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen electronics and 3D printing company founded 2015 by Chris Hong (with co-founder Kevin Wang); the name combines 'ELE' (electronic) and 'GOO' (googol). Best known for the Mars/Saturn resin printers, with FDM (Neptune, Centauri Carbon) and filament as a newer expansion. Elegoo appears to produce its own-brand filament directly and is the owner-verified manufacturer behind the Deeplee label. Catalog is unusually broad for a printer brand, running from budget PLA to flame-retardant PC and carbon/glass-filled composites.

manufacturers.name: Eryone (Shenzhen Eryone Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen filament producer founded in 2018 running a dual consumer and B2B/OEM business: it sells its own broad Eryone-branded range and white-labels filament for other brands, including ENISINA (project-owner verified). Also sells FDM and resin printers, resin and Maflex build surfaces.

manufacturers.name: eSUN (Shenzhen Esun Industrial Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Founded 2002 in Shenzhen, eSUN is one of the oldest and highest-volume Chinese filament and resin producers (~30,000 t/yr capacity, NEEQ-listed, stock 836514). It sells under its own eSUN brand and is a major upstream OEM whose production reaches many budget retail labels.

manufacturers.name: Extrudr (FD3D GmbH)
manufacturers.summary: Austrian filament manufacturer based in Lauterach, Vorarlberg, trading as Extrudr under the legal entity FD3D GmbH. Produces in Austria with in-house laser-micrometer diameter QC, and is best known for GreenTEC and GreenTEC Pro - oil-free, bio-based engineering materials positioned as sustainable alternatives to petrochemical polymers.

manufacturers.name: Fiberlogy (Fiberlab S.A.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament manufacturer near Krakow, trading as Fiberlogy under the legal entity Fiberlab S.A. Produces in-house in Poland with a 'Made in EU' marketing emphasis, and carries an unusually deep engineering and composite lineup (PCTG, PP, PA-CF) for its catalog size alongside decorative lines such as FiberSilk.

manufacturers.name: Filament PM (Plasty Mladec)
manufacturers.summary: Czech filament brand launched in 2013 by Plasty Mladec, a plastics extruder founded in 1992 that originally made plastic profiles and welding wire. Around 16 filament types in 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm, including carbon-fibre CFJet, wood-filled WoodJet and recycled RePLA+/RePETG lines, distributed to roughly 30 countries. An official Prusa Research filament partner since 2014.

manufacturers.name: Filamentive (Filamentive Limited)
manufacturers.summary: UK sustainability-focused filament brand in Bradford, built around post-industrial recycled feedstock from single-source waste streams. Range covers rPLA and rPETG in many variants plus TPU, ASA, PEEK and bio-derived Algae PLA, Hemp PLA and BioHT, offered in XL and refill spool formats. Certified to RoHS, REACH, ISO 14021 and EN-71, and an Ultimaker Material Alliance Partner.

manufacturers.name: Fillamentum Manufacturing Czech s.r.o.
manufacturers.summary: Czech filament manufacturer founded in 2011 in Hulin, originally trading as Parzlich s.r.o. Vertically integrated with in-house R&D and one of the broadest exotic-polymer catalogs in Europe (PVDF, PVC, PEBA, PC/ABS, PP). ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certified and, unusually for the sector, publicly traded on the Prague Stock Exchange under ticker FILL.

manufacturers.name: Zhejiang Flashforge 3D Technology Co., Ltd.
manufacturers.summary: Zhejiang-based printer maker founded 2011 (Creator, Adventurer, Guider, AD5X lines) that extrudes its own filament in-house. Flashforge is also the owner-verified manufacturer behind Voxelab, its budget consumer sub-brand. Filament catalog leans toward high-speed tuned commodity materials plus engineering-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced variants.

manufacturers.name: FormFutura B.V.
manufacturers.summary: Dutch filament supplier founded in 2012 by Arnold Medenblik, operating largely as a B2B/wholesale brand serving 400+ resellers in 75+ countries. Carries the broadest material catalog among the European premium brands surveyed, from budget EasyFil consumer spools through high-temperature engineering polymers (PEEK, PEI, PEKK, PPSU, PPS), plus resins and pellets.

manufacturers.name: Forward AM Technologies (Ultrafuse)
manufacturers.summary: Engineering-materials supplier behind the Ultrafuse filament brand, best known for pioneering print-then-sinter metal FDM filaments (Ultrafuse 316L and 17-4PH stainless steel) alongside a full polymer range. Formerly BASF Forward AM, it is NO LONGER part of BASF: BASF has exited additive manufacturing and Forward AM was carved out via management buyout into an independent company led by CEO Martin Back, retaining the Ultrafuse brand and IP.

manufacturers.name: Fusion Filaments
manufacturers.summary: Value-tier US filament seller based in Maryland Heights, Missouri, with a copolyester-heavy catalog (PCTG, HT-PET) alongside PLA, ABS and ASA and a government/school purchasing program. Whether it extrudes its own filament or sources it was not established from available pages.

manufacturers.name: GEEETECH (Shenzhen Getech Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen 3D printing manufacturer founded in 2013, one of the earliest Chinese open-source printer companies. It builds its own FDM printers, filament dryers and build surfaces alongside a broad filament range, and acts as an upstream OEM producing filament for the TEQStone, XZN and Giantarm labels (project-owner verified).

manufacturers.name: HATCHBOX 3D (Hatchbox Inc.)
manufacturers.summary: Long-running Amazon-first US filament label, trading since at least 2014 (HB HATCHBOX trademarks filed 2014/2015). Hatchbox is a brand/importer rather than a factory: standard lines have historically been described as Chinese-manufactured, while the separate PLA MAX line is marketed as USA-made. No specific OEM has been confirmed.

manufacturers.name: IC3D, Inc. (IC3D Printers)
manufacturers.summary: Central Ohio manufacturer founded in 2012, vertically integrated across "machines, materials, and manufacturing": it extrudes its own filament in-house and also designs and builds its own industrial FDM printers (Virago series, up to 4 cubic feet of build volume). Also sells production-focused additive manufacturing and contract manufacturing services.

manufacturers.name: IEMAI 3D (Dongguan Imai Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Dongguan-based manufacturer established 2015 producing 3D printing materials and equipment for industrial sectors, and the parent OEM behind the iSanghu and iSanmate retail filament labels. Consumer output skews toward aesthetic and visual-effect filaments rather than production-grade engineering materials.

manufacturers.name: igus GmbH
manufacturers.summary: Cologne-based German motion-plastics manufacturer whose iglidur tribo-polymer line extends into 3D printing as 'tribo-filament'. Its filaments are engineered for wear resistance, self-lubrication and low friction in functional moving parts — gears, bushings, cable carriers — rather than for general prototyping. Vertically integrated: igus compounds its own polymers and extrudes its own filament.

manufacturers.name: Inland (Micro Center)
manufacturers.summary: Private store brand of US electronics retailer Micro Center, with no separate corporate entity, website or social presence. Inland filament is produced by eSUN or Polymaker (project-owner verified), identifiable by the spool cutout: diamond = Polymaker, round = eSUN. The catalogue mirrors those OEMs' own lines at Micro Center's budget in-store pricing.

manufacturers.name: Jamg He
manufacturers.summary: Chinese materials and hardware producer with over two decades in UV-curing and 3D printing, selling FDM filaments, SLA/LCD/DLP resins, LCD printers, UV ink, curing boxes and dryers. It is the manufacturer behind the AceAddity retail filament label.

manufacturers.name: Jayo
manufacturers.summary: Budget AliExpress/Amazon filament label sold through its own storefronts, positioned as a cheaper alternative to Sunlu-branded product. Jayo is not a factory: its filament is manufactured by Sunlu, so its material originates from Sunlu's Chinese production bases.

manufacturers.name: Keene Village Plastics (Village Plastics)
manufacturers.summary: Long-established US industrial plastics manufacturer that extruded its way into 3D printing filament at wholesale scale, self-describing as "the largest manufacturer of high-quality 3D printer filaments in the United States". Operates consumer-facing as Village Plastics and reached the hobbyist market by acquiring the MakeShaper filament brand in 2018/2019.

manufacturers.name: Kexcelled (North Bridge New Material Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Suzhou-based filament and resin manufacturer selling directly under the Kexcelled brand, with an unusually strong certification profile for a value-priced Chinese producer (ISO 9001, ISO 13485 medical QMS, FDA and CE-MDR Class I, UL 94 V0 on select materials) and manufacturing diversified beyond China into Thailand.

manufacturers.name: Kimya (ARMOR Group)
manufacturers.summary: French engineering-filament brand of the ARMOR Group industrial group, positioned for functional end-use parts rather than hobbyist printing. Best documented product is ABS-R, an impact-modified ABS; the broader catalog reportedly spans PLA, PETG, TPU, nylon (including reinforced grades), PC and carbon/glass-fiber-filled engineering materials.

manufacturers.name: Kingroon (Kingroon 3D)
manufacturers.summary: Budget Chinese printer brand (KP3S, KLP1) that also sells a wide house filament catalog. Kingroon does not extrude its own filament: per owner-verified records it is manufactured by Landu in China, and a third-party review source independently characterises Kingroon filament as an OEM brand attached to the printers, corroborating the contract-manufacture pattern without naming Landu. Positioning is firmly budget, with bulk 10kg pricing and occasional batch-to-batch variability reported.

manufacturers.name: Landu (Hongkong Landu Innovations Technology Co., Limited)
manufacturers.summary: Hong Kong-registered filament company with large-scale production in Shenzhen and Dongguan — a 50,000 sq m manufacturing centre running roughly 3,000 tons per month. Sells budget-priced LANDU-branded filament, resin and accessories, and is the confirmed OEM behind Kingroon-branded filament.

manufacturers.name: MatterHackers, Inc.
manufacturers.summary: One of the largest US 3D-printing retailers, based in Lake Forest, California. MatterHackers is primarily a marketplace for third-party printers and materials — and owns/operates the LulzBot printer brand — but also sells house-brand filament under Pro Series (engineering tier) and MH Build Series (budget tier), claimed as made in the USA.

manufacturers.name: NinjaTek (Fenner Precision Polymers)
manufacturers.summary: Flexible-filament specialist operating as a division of Fenner Precision Polymers, part of Fenner (UK), which Michelin Group acquired in May 2018. Its catalog is almost entirely TPU — NinjaFlex, Chinchilla, Cheetah, Eel and Armadillo — extruded in the US on the back of Fenner's roughly 50 years of belt and polymer extrusion experience. It also retails colorFabb-branded materials through its own shop.

manufacturers.name: Overture 3D Technologies, LLC
manufacturers.summary: US-based consumer filament brand founded in 2019 and headquartered in Houston, Texas. Overture is an importer/brand rather than a factory: its filament is manufactured by Polymaker (project-owner verified), so the material itself originates in China. Best known as a high-volume Amazon budget/mid brand with a broad PLA aesthetic range.

manufacturers.name: Polymaker
manufacturers.summary: R&D-led filament manufacturer headquartered in Changshu, China, with offices in Shanghai, Utrecht and Houston. Its catalog spans budget aesthetic PLA (PolyTerra/Panchroma) through engineering composites (Fiberon, PolyMax), and it is one of very few Chinese-origin brands with confirmed US manufacturing capacity.

manufacturers.name: Protopasta (Protoplant, Inc.)
manufacturers.summary: Protoplant, Inc. (dba "Protoplant, makers of Protopasta") is a US specialty filament maker founded in 2013 via Kickstarter by Dustin Cram, Aaron Cram and Alexander Dick. It extrudes all of its own product in Vancouver, Washington and is best known as an early pioneer of composite and filled PLA rather than a broad engineering-material catalog.

manufacturers.name: Prusa Research a.s. (Prusament)
manufacturers.summary: Czech joint-stock company behind the Original Prusa printer ecosystem. Its filament brand, Prusament, is extruded in-house by wholly-owned subsidiary Prusa Polymers a.s. on roughly 12 production lines near Prague. Vertically integrated: Prusa makes its own filament, printers and build surfaces, and no evidence was found of it white-labelling for other brands.

manufacturers.name: Push Plastic
manufacturers.summary: US filament extruder established September 2013, running its own production since inception and claiming 25+ years of plastics experience behind it. Unusually broad engineering catalog for a small US operation — PEI, PMMA and PC+PBT alongside the commodity materials — in both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm, with SAM.gov certification for government and institutional sales.

manufacturers.name: QIDI Tech (Zhejiang Qidi Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Chinese printer maker selling under the QIDI / Qidi Tech consumer brand, known for actively-heated-chamber machines (X-Max, Q1 series). Its filament is a house accessory line sold almost exclusively through qidi3d.com rather than third-party retail, and is profiled specifically for QIDI's own printers. No third-party OEM relationship is confirmed and the brand does not appear in the owner-verified ground-truth table, so whether production is truly in-house or contract-manufactured remains open.

manufacturers.name: Real Filament
manufacturers.summary: Dutch filament brand describing itself as 'a Dutch company that produces 3D filament within Europe'. Around eight filament types listed without distinct line branding - PLA (including a biodegradable/pliable variant), PETG, TPU, PVA, a water-soluble support and a 'multifunctional durable' material - sold from NL stock and through a reseller network in the Netherlands and UK.

manufacturers.name: ROSA3D (ROSA PLAST Sp. z o.o.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament manufacturer in Hipolitow near Warsaw, self-described as a 'Polish manufacturer of 3D printing filament'. Broad catalogue spanning PLA, PET-G (including a high-speed grade), PCTG, ABS, ASA, PC, TPU, PA (incl. PA12+CF), PP/PP-GF30, HIPS and an R-Series recycled range, with specialty ESD-safe, medical-grade and PTFE-infused grades.

manufacturers.name: Shenzhen Snapmaker Technologies Co., Ltd.
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen company founded 2016, distinctive for building multi-function 3-in-1 machines (3D printing, laser, CNC) rather than printers alone (Snapmaker 2.0, Artisan, J1, U1). Filament is an in-house accessory line with RFID-tagged spools tuned to Snapmaker's own machines, and the material range is narrower than pure filament brands — PLA, PETG and TPU only, with no confirmed ABS/ASA/PA/PC lines. No third-party OEM relationship is documented and the brand is absent from the owner-verified ground-truth table.

manufacturers.name: Spectrum Filaments (Spectrum Group Sp. z o.o.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament manufacturer near Warsaw that debuted in 2015 and now lists 50+ materials, from commodity PLA and PET-G through PCTG, PA, PP, PC, PPS, PEBA and soluble supports, plus pellets and a spool refill system. States that all filament is produced in-house in Poland, and is expanding into North America with a dedicated US warehouse and store.

manufacturers.name: Sunlu (Zhuhai Sunlu Industrial Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Founded July 2013 in Zhuhai, Guangdong, Sunlu is a high-volume Chinese filament producer with three FDM production bases, 20,000+ tons of cumulative shipments and 36 global distribution points. It sells under its own brand, is well known for its S-series filament dryers, and manufactures for several budget retail labels.

manufacturers.name: taulman3D
manufacturers.summary: One of the earliest specialty-nylon FDM filament brands, historically based in Missouri, USA, and known for Nylon 645, Nylon 680 FDA, Alloy 910, Nylon Bridge and the T-Glase copolyester line. Acquired by Brazilian petrochemical major Braskem, which now hosts the taulman3D catalog on its braskem3d.com additive-manufacturing portal alongside Braskem's own PP/PE and bio-based filaments.

manufacturers.name: Tinmorry
manufacturers.summary: Budget filament label distributed largely through Amazon and its own storefronts, emphasising metallic and silk specialty finishes alongside standard PLA and PETG. No legal entity or factory was identified; third-party reviews repeatedly flag batch-to-batch consistency problems.

manufacturers.name: UltiMaker (Ultimaker B.V.)
manufacturers.summary: Dutch desktop and professional FDM printer maker that also formulates and sells its own verified material range (Tough PLA, CPE/CPE+, Nylon, PC, TPU 95A, PVA, PP and more). Headquartered in Utrecht since 2019; the 2022 merger with MakerBot brought that brand in-house, leaving NPM Capital with 53.5% and Stratasys with 46.5%. Runs an open materials marketplace with third-party partners such as Tectonic-3D on top of its own catalog.

manufacturers.name: Voxelab
manufacturers.summary: Budget consumer sub-brand of Zhejiang Flashforge 3D Technology Co., Ltd., best known historically for the Aquila printer line. Voxelab is a label rather than an independent extruder: its filament is manufactured by Flashforge in China, a relationship that is owner-verified, self-disclosed on Voxelab's own about page, and even visible in the brand's Amazon storefront name ('Voxelab Official: Flashforge 3D Printer'). Manufacturing countries here therefore reflect Flashforge's Zhejiang facilities.

manufacturers.name: Ziro (ZIRO 3D Print Technology Company Limited)
manufacturers.summary: Hong Kong-registered brand with production in Shenzhen, differentiated by an unusually broad range of exotic and novelty aesthetic PLA finishes rather than engineering materials. Ziro also runs its own published OEM/private-label and wholesale programme, so it likely supplies unnamed third-party labels.

plates.name: Textured PEI (powder-coated spring steel)
plates.summary: The modern default build surface: powder-coated polyetherimide on flexible spring steel. Grips hot, releases cold, needs no adhesives for most materials, and leaves a uniform textured finish. Example entry pending Phase D research.
plates.surface_makeup: Polyetherimide (PEI) powder coating fused onto a spring-steel sheet
